structured_output.summary:
I found no public CIFAR-100 speedrun submission that beats the tree's ~4.47 s tip. The public CIFAR-100 forks hold only the template. futurebiohackers (75.29% in 8.11 s) remains the only published external recipe, and it dropped Muon, which the tree has already shown was a mistake on this setup. The external evidence that matters is below.

(1) Late layer freezing (H2.20). The evidence is mixed but leans slightly in favour of the "randomized/partial" variants. Drop-Muon (2510.02239) truncates backprop below a randomly sampled start layer per step, shifting probability from shallow to deep layers over training. It reports up to 1.4x wall-clock speed-ups on small CNNs, but only on MNIST/Fashion-MNIST, plus a weaker 'earlier to 90% train accuracy' result on CIFAR-10, with no test numbers. MosaicML's replication found ~5% throughput and explicitly 'no evidence' of a better quality/speed trade-off, although its CIFAR-100 ResNet-56 run gained +0.4 pp. E116's ~0.03 pp per 1% fits this picture: freezing works as a rate lever, not as a free gain.

(2) Averaging (H9.2). Neither CIFAR-10 SOTA recipe (hiverge, Fable e1) nor airbench94_muon uses a training-time lookahead. airbench's SGD lookahead uses a cubic alpha ramp (decay = 0.95^5 * (t/T)^3, every 5 steps), so it does almost no smoothing early and the most at the end. The tip's every-3-steps lookahead is a different shape, and that shape is a natural H9.2 arm.

(3) Noise (H4.8). Jordan's variance paper (2304.01910) shows that run-to-run spread is mostly finite-test-set sampling, and that trainings make roughly independent errors. That matches E113 (pairing gave no variance reduction). It argues against a persistent recipe x seed offset on seeds 0-2, so E100's gate passes look like luck plus a ~0.3 pp population margin.

(4) Schedule shape (H7.4). There is weak external support for a stable phase on CIFAR-100: in 2602.06797, ResNet-18/SGD on CIFAR-100 preferred a decay over the last 40% of training, while an easy binary task preferred immediate decay. That regime (bs 20, 5 epochs, ~12.5k steps) is far from ours.

(5) Augmentation (H12). Gains from multiple augmentation samples at fixed batch size only appear in long runs. The 23-epoch result comes from 'Augment your batch', which adds compute per step. CIFAR-10 SOTA recipes do use brightness/contrast jitter and LS 0.09, but those were tested here under SGD (E008) and Muon (E037) and lost.

(6) The airbench paper's ~20% FLOP cut came from making the first conv in each block 2x2, and it gave no A100 wall-clock gain. That is a prior against H2.18 depth cuts.

findings.claim: Drop-Muon (Randomized Progressive Training): each step samples a minimum layer index s^k and updates only layers s^k..b. Backprop is truncated, so 'no gradients are computed' for the frozen shallower layers. An 'epoch-shift distribution' moves probability mass from shallow to deep start indices over training, so shallow layers are frozen more and more often late. Reports reaching equal accuracy up to 1.4x faster wall-clock on MNIST (~1.2x on Fashion-MNIST). On CIFAR-10 with a 3-layer CNN [128,256,512] it only reports reaching 90% train accuracy earlier, with no test accuracy given.
findings.relevance: This is a stochastic version of E116's late group-1/stem freeze. Instead of one hard freeze at 85%, group 1 could be detached on a growing fraction of steps over, say, the last 40-50%, with the same total saving. That may spread the -0.12 pp loss more cheaply. It needs both graph variants warmed for each flag combination (the E115 lesson). Evidence is weak: tiny CNNs and training-accuracy metrics only.

findings.claim: MosaicML layer freezing: ~5% throughput gain on ResNet-50/ImageNet with a 0.5-1% accuracy drop. ResNet-56 on CIFAR-100: ~5% speed and +0.4 pp (75.82 -> 76.22), not replicated. The card states 'There is No Evidence that Layer Freezing Improves the Tradeoff Between Model Quality and Training Speed.' It recommends freeze_start >= 0.1.
findings.relevance: Matches E116 (-3.6% time, -0.12 pp, ~0.03 pp per 1%): freezing is a rate lever comparable to schedule trims, not a free gain. A later freeze (90-92%) should keep about the same rate. It only beats the trims if the time saving per frozen step is larger than in E116.

findings.claim: FreezeOut reports up to 20% wall-clock savings with no accuracy loss for ResNets on CIFAR, 3% loss for DenseNets, and no improvement for VGG.
findings.relevance: Our net is VGG-like (airbench). FreezeOut's null VGG result and MosaicML's null Pareto result lower the prior that freezing does better than its E116 rate.

findings.claim: airbench lookahead: every 5 steps, ema = decay*ema + (1-decay)*net and net <- ema, with decay = 0.95^5 * (step/total)^3. Smoothing is near zero early and grows cubically to ~0.77 at the end. Lookahead cut the epochs needed from 18 to 12.0 (~33%) in airbench94's SGD regime.
findings.relevance: This is the reference design the tip's SGD-era lookahead comes from. The cubic decay exponent and cadence (every 3 steps at bs 1536 on the tip) were never tuned under Muon. Natural H9.2.1 arms: change the ramp exponent (e.g. power 2 or 4) or the peak decay at fixed cadence, not just a uniform alpha x0.7/x1.3. E092 showed lookahead carries ~0.2-0.3 pp, so its shape plausibly matters.

findings.claim: hiverge's CIFAR-10 SOTA recipe has no lookahead or EMA. It uses bs 1536, ~7.65 epochs, Muon lr 0.205 with momentum 0.655 (Nesterov), linear decay to 0, LS 0.09, brightness 0.1399 and contrast 0.1308 jitter, translate 2, whitening bias trained 0.2 epoch, BN weights frozen (requires_grad=False), and TTA level 2.
findings.relevance: Under Muon, CIFAR-10 SOTA gets by without training-time weight averaging. On CIFAR-100, E092 shows removing lookahead costs ~0.2 pp, so that difference probably reflects CIFAR-100's noisier, under-fit regime. It also confirms that freezing BN weights is standard. Whether the tip trains BN weights is worth a code check: if it does, freezing them is a small free cut of per-step optimizer traffic (H2.4).

findings.claim: Fable e1: final EMA every 4 steps over the last 8 steps with decay 0.7, written back to the net. Uses 3 epochs each at 24/28/32 px (8.875 epochs), bs 1536, Muon-style lr 0.2255 / momentum 0.655, SGD bias lr 0.0573 / head lr 0.5415 at momentum 0.825, LS 0.09, decay over 8.5 epochs to a 0.05 floor, and widths 64->256->256 with 2 convs per block.
findings.relevance: Confirms the tip's tail design matches Fable's. Fable uses 2 convs per block at much smaller widths, which is the external 2-conv reference for H2.18. Its CIFAR-10 schedule spends 3 epochs at 28 px, where the tree found 28 px no better than trims (E090).

findings.claim: Jordan (2023): repeated trainings show large test-set variance but little variance on the underlying distribution. Runs make approximately independent errors on test examples, and the variance follows from class calibration. airbench94 (10,000 runs): test-set sd 0.128-0.157%, with distribution-wise variance 5-9x lower.
findings.relevance: Explains E113: pairing seeds across recipes gives no variance reduction because errors are nearly independent per run. It argues against H4.8's 'persistent recipe x seed offset on seeds 0-2'. Any recipe change re-draws the per-seed errors, so E100's seeds-0-2 advantage is most likely luck, and the gate is passed by population margin (~0.753) plus chance. It also confirms that only more seeds, not more processes, reduce comparison noise (H4.6).

findings.claim: Warmup-stable-decay on CIFAR-100: ResNet-18 trained from scratch with SGD (momentum 0.9, bs 20, peak lr 0.2, 5 epochs, 10% warmup). Decay fractions r in {0.2..1.0} were tested. CIFAR-100 (100 classes) preferred r=0.4, a stable phase followed by decay over the last 40%. An easy binary CIFAR task preferred decay right after warmup (r=1). The excerpt gives no accuracy deltas.
findings.relevance: The first image-classification evidence that harder tasks such as CIFAR-100 favour a stable phase, which raises H7.4's prior slightly. The regime (~12.5k tiny-batch SGD steps) differs greatly from ~280 Muon steps with lookahead, so transfer is uncertain. If H7.4.1 runs, test decay over the last ~40-50%, as already specified.

findings.claim: Fort et al.: at fixed batch size, augmentation multiplicity >1 still improves test accuracy even though each batch holds fewer unique images. The highlighted short-budget result (ResNet-44, CIFAR-10, Cutout, 94.15% in 23 epochs vs 93.07% at 100 epochs) comes from the larger-batch 'Augment your batch' setting, which adds compute per step.
findings.relevance: For H12.1.1 (fixed compute, ~7.5 epochs), no fixed-compute short-budget evidence was found, so the prior stays low (~0.08). The paper's own finding that augmentation matters more with fewer unique examples is a weak argument that multiplicity could help.

findings.claim: airbench96 reaches 79.76% on CIFAR-100 (with Cutout, 40-ish epochs, no retuning) vs 78.04% for ResNet-18. Translate 2 is standard, and Cutout (12 px) is used only for the 96% CIFAR-10 target at long budgets. No ablation of translate magnitude or Cutout across epoch budgets. Quote: 'we can lower the FLOPs of airbench96 by almost 20% by reducing the kernel size of the first convolution in each block from 3 to 2 and increasing epochs from 40 to 45. But this does not improve the wallclock training time on an A100.' Whitening biases: 'trained for 3 epochs, after which we disable their gradient to increase backward-pass throughput'.
findings.relevance: No external support for stronger translation at short budgets (H12.3 stays low). The FLOP-cut quote is the main external prior against depth and kernel cuts (H2.18) on A100. Our runs are energy-bound at 32 px, though, so FLOP cuts may transfer better here than on airbench's setup. Profile untimed first, as H2.18.1 already says.

findings.claim: The only public CIFAR-100 speedrun result found is 75.29% in 8.11 s (A100-SXM4, airbench-derived). That team reports 'Muon lost to SGD at every size' and removed it. The AIDDA-Institute repo has no PRs, and the forks (RyanChong0117, Daniel-T-S-Adams) contain only the template; the AIDDA ResNet9 baseline is 75.36% in 59.3 s.
findings.relevance: No external recipe beats the tree's ~4.47 s tip, so remaining gains must come from the tree's own levers (freeze rate, averaging shape, profiled depth/width).
